claims.text: Human resource management is the business function responsible for planning, recruiting, developing, rewarding and retaining the people a business needs in order to meet its objectives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The role of HRM is to turn organisational objectives into workforce requirements - how many people are needed, holding which skills, at what times and at what labour cost - and then to supply and maintain that workforce.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: HRM contributes to organisational objectives along four routes: putting the right number of people with the right skills in place, raising output per employee through training and motivation, holding labour costs to what the plan allows, and keeping the workforce willing to stay and the business compliant with employment law.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: HRM works on objectives indirectly: it changes what the workforce is able to do and willing to do, and the objective is then met by the workforce doing it, so an HRM decision shows up in output, cost or quality only after the workforce behaves differently.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Recruiting and training take months rather than days, so a business whose objectives change quickly can find its workforce lagging behind its plans; the longer the lead time on a skill, the earlier the HRM decision has to be taken.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How much HRM contributes to an objective depends on how far that objective rests on people: a business competing on service quality or specialist skill depends more on HRM decisions than one whose output is set mainly by machinery.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A workforce plan is a statement of how many employees a business expects to need, with which skills and at what times, together with the actions it intends to take to close the gap between that requirement and the workforce it currently holds.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A workforce plan is built in three steps: forecast the workforce the business will require from its sales and output plans, audit the workforce it already has by number and skill, and set out the shortfall or surplus that the plan must close.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The reasons a business prepares a workforce plan include expected change in demand, a change in technology or working methods that alters the skills required, known retirements and expected resignations, and the lead time needed to recruit or train a scarce skill.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The role of a workforce plan is to convert a forecast into dated actions - recruit, train, redeploy or reduce numbers - so that a shortage is filled before it stops output and a surplus is dealt with before it is paid for over a long period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A workforce plan uses the labour turnover rate to forecast replacement recruitment: a business of 240 employees losing 7.5% a year has to plan to replace about 18 people a year before it recruits anyone for growth.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A workforce plan rests on a demand forecast, so its usefulness falls as that forecast becomes less reliable; where demand is volatile, businesses tend to plan against a range of outcomes, or to use flexible contracts and overtime, rather than commit to one number of permanent posts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour turnover is the proportion of a business's workforce that leaves and has to be replaced over a period, normally measured over one year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour turnover (%) = (number of employees leaving during the period / average number of employees during the period) x 100, where the numerator counts leavers of every kind and the denominator is the average headcount over the same period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A Windhoek logistics firm employs an average of 240 people over a year and 18 leave. Its labour turnover is 18 / 240 = 0.075, which is 7.5% for the year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The denominator is the average number employed over the period, not the headcount at the start or at the end; in a business whose size is changing quickly the two give different answers, and the average is the figure the measure is defined on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour turnover is a rate expressed as a percentage of the workforce, not a count of people, so two businesses that lose the same number of employees have different turnover rates if they differ in size.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A turnover figure records how many people left, not why they left, so on its own it identifies that something may be wrong without identifying what; exit interviews, pay comparisons with local employers and workload evidence are what turn the rate into a decision.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: High labour turnover raises spending on recruitment and induction, removes the experience the leavers held, and can lower the output of those who remain while vacancies are unfilled and while replacements are still learning the job.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: High labour turnover also has effects a business may want: it brings in people with new skills and fresh thinking, it moves out employees who were performing poorly, and it allows numbers to fall by non-replacement rather than by redundancy, so the same rate can be damaging in one business and useful in another.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Low labour turnover keeps experience in the business and holds recruitment spending down, but where it falls very low it can leave a workforce short of new ideas and block promotion for employees already inside, which can itself push ambitious staff to leave.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether a particular turnover rate is a problem depends on the norm for the sector, the skill level involved and the cost of replacing one leaver: a rate that is ordinary for seasonal retail work would be serious in a business whose employees take a year to become fully productive.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Rising labour turnover feeds back into the workforce plan, because every unplanned leaver adds a recruitment and induction cost and a period of reduced output that the plan has to allow for.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Recruitment is the process of identifying a vacancy and attracting a field of suitable applicants from which a selection can then be made.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The recruitment process runs in order: confirm that the vacancy exists and establish what the job requires, write a job description, write a person specification, choose a recruitment method and place the vacancy, then receive and acknowledge applications.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A job description sets out the title, purpose, duties, responsibilities, reporting lines and working conditions of a post - it describes the job, not the person who will hold it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A person specification sets out the qualifications, skills, experience and personal attributes an applicant needs in order to do the job, normally separated into essential requirements and desirable ones.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The two recruitment documents are used at different points: the job description tells applicants what they would be doing and later underpins the employment contract and any appraisal, while the person specification supplies the criteria against which applications are screened and candidates compared.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because the person specification supplies the screening criteria, a specification listing requirements the job does not actually need narrows the field without improving the appointment, and can screen out applicants who could have done the work well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The recruitment methods named in this topic are job advertisements placed in newspapers, on radio or on notice boards, employment agencies that hold registers of candidates and screen on the employer's behalf, and online recruitment through job boards, the business's own website and professional networks.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A job advertisement reaches a wide and undirected audience, so it can attract applicants the business would not otherwise have found, but every unsuitable application it produces has to be read and screened, and the cost of the advertisement is paid whether or not a good field results.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An employment agency saves the employer screening time and can reach candidates who are not actively looking, because it holds a register and approaches people directly; the employer pays a fee, often set as a percentage of the first year's salary, and the shortlist reflects the agency's reading of the person specification rather than the employer's own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Online recruitment is cheap for each applicant reached and fast to place, and it can produce very large numbers of applications, which moves the employer's work from attracting applicants to filtering them; it reaches only applicants with reliable internet access and the confidence to apply online, which in parts of Namibia leaves rural applicants outside the field.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Choice of recruitment method follows the post, because the three named methods differ in cost, in reach and in how much screening the employer has to do: a scarce senior skill is often handled through an agency or a professional network, while a local unskilled vacancy may be filled from a notice at the premises or an advertisement in a local newspaper.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal recruitment fills a vacancy from among people the business already employs, by promotion or by transfer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External recruitment fills a vacancy from outside the business, from applicants who are not currently employed by it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal recruitment is usually quicker and cheaper because the candidate's performance is already known and only the new duties need to be learned, and the visible prospect of promotion can raise the effort of other employees; against that, the promotion leaves a second vacancy to fill and brings in no thinking from outside.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: External recruitment widens the field and can bring in skills and experience the business does not hold; it costs more in advertising and selection time, the appointee takes longer to reach full productivity because everything about the business is new, and the evidence about the candidate is less reliable than an internal record of performance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where the skills a post needs do not exist inside the business, external recruitment is the only route that can fill it and the cost comparison does not decide the question; where the skills do exist inside, the comparison of cost, speed and effect on motivation is what decides it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selection is the process of choosing, from the applicants that recruitment has attracted, the one whose evidence best matches the person specification.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The selection methods named in this topic - curriculum vitae or resume, application form, interview, reference, testing and assessment centre - are normally combined rather than used alone, because each produces a different kind of evidence about an applicant and each has a weakness the others can cover.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A curriculum vitae, also called a resume, is a document written by the applicant summarising personal details, qualifications, employment history, skills and referees.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because the applicant writes the curriculum vitae and chooses its format, it shows what that applicant decides to present and in whatever order flatters them most, which makes direct comparison between applicants slower and means the claims on it are evidence to be checked rather than facts established.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An application form is a document written by the employer which every applicant completes, asking the same questions in the same order.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because the employer sets the questions, application forms make applicants directly comparable point by point and force an answer on matters a curriculum vitae can quietly omit, such as a gap between jobs; they take longer to complete than sending an existing curriculum vitae, which can reduce the number of applications from people who are not short of other offers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An interview is a structured conversation in which the employer questions an applicant to test the evidence in the application, explore how the applicant thinks and judge suitability for the post.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An interview tests communication and manner directly and lets the employer follow up an answer, which no written method does; the judgement rests on a short meeting and is open to interviewer bias, and using a set list of job-related questions with more than one interviewer reduces that weakness without removing it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A reference is a statement about an applicant's past performance, conduct or reliability, obtained by the employer from a previous employer or another named person who has known the applicant in a working capacity.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A reference verifies claims made elsewhere in an application and comes from someone who has seen the applicant work, which the written methods cannot offer; referees are chosen by the applicant and many employers limit what they are prepared to confirm in writing, so a reference more often rules an applicant out than separates two strong ones.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Testing in selection means setting applicants a standardised task - an aptitude test, a skills or practical test, or a psychometric test - and scoring every applicant on the same basis.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A test gives a directly comparable measure of something the job needs, which an interview can only infer from what an applicant says; the evidence is worth only as much as the test's fit to the job, and a test measuring something the post does not require separates applicants on a basis that has nothing to do with the work.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An assessment centre is an extended selection event, usually lasting one or more days, at which a group of applicants is observed by several assessors across several exercises such as group tasks, presentations, tests and interviews.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because an assessment centre gathers evidence from several exercises and several assessors, one weak performance or one assessor's prejudice carries less weight in the final decision than it does in a single interview; the method is expensive in assessors' time, venue and applicants' time, which tends to confine it to senior posts and to large graduate intakes where the cost is spread over several appointments.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How much selection effort is worth spending depends on the cost of appointing the wrong person: where a mistake means a short notice period and a quick replacement, a form and one interview may be enough, and where it means a year of poor decisions or a long training investment, a longer process can pay for itself.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An employment contract is the agreement between employer and employee setting out the terms on which work is done, including duties, hours, pay, holiday entitlement, notice periods and the type and length of the engagement.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contract types differ in the security they give the employee and the flexibility they leave the employer: a permanent contract commits the business to a continuing cost and gives the employee steady income, while fixed-term, temporary, part-time and zero-hours or casual arrangements let the business match labour to demand and leave the employee's income less certain.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because a contract that gives the employer flexibility gives the employee less certain income, employees on casual and short fixed-term contracts tend to leave as soon as steadier work is available, so a business that staffs a core function this way often carries higher labour turnover and repeated recruitment cost as the price of flexibility.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The exact rights an employment contract carries - minimum notice, minimum wage, maximum hours, what has to be recorded in writing - are set by the employment law of the country where the work is done, so the general principle transfers between countries but any specific entitlement does not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Contract choice belongs to workforce planning as well as to law, because the mix of permanent and flexible contracts fixes both the labour cost the business is committed to and the speed at which it can change the size of its workforce when demand moves.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Redundancy is the ending of employment because the job itself is no longer required - the post disappears, through closure, falling output or a change in methods, and the employee has not done anything wrong.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Dismissal is the ending of employment by the employer because of the employee's own conduct or capability; the job continues to exist and the business intends someone else to do it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The first difference between redundancy and dismissal is what has ended: in redundancy the post has gone and the person was adequate, in dismissal the post remains and the person was not, which is why the two carry different payments and different procedures.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Voluntary redundancy means employees are invited to volunteer to leave, normally in return for a payment, while involuntary or compulsory redundancy means the employer selects who goes, using criteria it has stated in advance.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Voluntary redundancy avoids the resentment that compulsory selection creates among those who stay, but the employees most willing to volunteer are often those most confident of finding other work, so a business can lose experience and skills it wanted to keep.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A dismissal is fair where the reason is one the law of that country recognises - such as persistent misconduct, incapability or a genuine operational reason - and the employer has followed a proper procedure of investigation, warning, a hearing and a right of appeal; it is unfair where the reason is not acceptable in law or the procedure was not followed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The distinction has direct financial consequences: an employee made redundant is normally entitled to a redundancy payment, an employee fairly dismissed is normally not, and an employee found to have been unfairly dismissed may be awarded compensation or reinstatement by a labour court or tribunal.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which reasons count as fair, what procedure has to be followed and how any redundancy payment is calculated are set by national employment law and differ between countries, so what the topic requires is the general distinction rather than the rules of any one jurisdiction.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employee morale is the general level of confidence, satisfaction and willingness to work that a workforce holds, shown in how readily employees attend, cooperate and put effort into work that is not directly supervised.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employee welfare refers to what a business provides for employees' physical and mental wellbeing beyond pay - safe working conditions, access to health provision, rest and eating facilities, and support during illness, injury or bereavement.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Work-life balance is the relationship between the time and effort an employee gives to work and the time left for the rest of their life; HRM policies that support it include flexible starting and finishing times, remote or hybrid working, part-time and job-share options, and limits on expected overtime.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: HRM practices that raise morale and welfare tend to reduce absence and labour turnover and to raise the effort employees put into work, which shows up as higher output per employee and lower recruitment spending; the effect is larger where output depends on judgement and discretionary effort than where the pace of work is set by a machine.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The relationship runs in both directions: poor morale raises absence and turnover, and high turnover then lowers morale further among those who remain, because their workload rises and established teams are broken up.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Welfare provision and work-life-balance policies cost money now and can reduce the hours available for output in the short run, while the turnover, absence and productivity gains appear later and are harder to attribute, so a business judging them has to compare a certain present cost against a probable future saving.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Workplace diversity means a workforce whose members differ from one another - in gender, age, ethnicity, language, background, physical ability and working experience.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Equality in the workplace means that employment decisions - recruitment, pay, training, promotion and dismissal - are made on the basis of what the job requires rather than on personal characteristics that have nothing to do with doing it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business that recruits and promotes on job-related criteria draws on the whole labour market rather than part of it, which widens the field for every vacancy and raises the chance that the strongest available applicant is the one appointed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A diverse workforce brings a wider range of experience to a problem and can read a wider range of customers, which matters most where the customer base is itself varied; the same differences can slow decisions and raise the effort needed to communicate clearly, so the gain depends on how the business manages the differences rather than on their presence.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Treating employees unequally on grounds unrelated to the job exposes a business to legal claims and to damage to its reputation as an employer, which can shrink the field of applicants for future vacancies and raise what it has to pay to fill them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which characteristics are legally protected, and what an employer is required to do about equality and representation, are set by the law of each country and differ between them, so the business case for equality and the legal duty are separate arguments and only the first transfers across borders.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training is the provision of instruction and practice that gives employees the knowledge and skills a job requires; the three forms named in this topic are induction, on-the-job and off-the-job training.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Induction training is the training given to a new employee at the start of employment, covering the business and its rules, the duties of the post, the people the employee will work with, and health and safety requirements.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Induction shortens the time before a new employee becomes productive and reduces early leaving, because a large share of early resignations follows from a new employee not understanding what is expected or not settling among colleagues; it takes the time of the person delivering it and delays the new employee's first productive day.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: On-the-job training is training carried out at the workplace while the employee does the actual job, usually by watching an experienced colleague, being coached by one, or rotating through the tasks of a section.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: On-the-job training is relatively cheap because no separate venue or outside trainer is needed and the trainee keeps producing while learning; its quality depends on the practice of whoever does the training, so poor habits pass on with good ones, and the experienced employee's own output falls while they teach.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Off-the-job training is training carried out away from the immediate work position - at a training centre, a college, or with an external provider - so that the employee is not producing while learning.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Off-the-job training gives access to specialist expertise, equipment and recognised qualifications that the business cannot supply from inside, and it lets the employee learn without production pressure or interruption; it costs more per employee, removes the employee from output for the whole period, and what is learned in general terms still has to be transferred to the business's own methods.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The choice between on-the-job and off-the-job training follows the skill being taught: a task specific to the business's own equipment and customers is usually learned fastest beside someone already doing it, while a qualification, or a skill nobody inside the business holds, has to be brought in from outside.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employee development is the longer-term broadening of an employee's capability beyond the demands of the current job, so that the employee can take on different or larger roles later.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training raises the skill with which a task is performed, which tends to raise output per employee, cut the rate of errors, waste and rework, and reduce accidents; it can also raise morale, because employees who can do a job well find it less stressful and see that the business is investing in them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Training is a cost before it is a benefit: the spending and the lost production come first and the productivity gain follows, and the gain is captured only for as long as the trained employee stays, which is why businesses that train heavily tend to work on retention at the same time.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The risk that a trained employee is recruited by a competitor is real, but on its own it is a weak reason not to train, because the untrained alternative carries its own cost in errors and low output; the risk is usually managed through pay and promotion routes, and, where the law of the country permits it, agreements that an employee repays part of the cost of a qualification if they leave soon after gaining it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Intrapreneurship is entrepreneurial behaviour by employees inside an existing business - spotting opportunities, proposing new products, services or methods, and taking responsibility for developing them, using the business's own resources rather than starting a separate venture.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employee development encourages intrapreneurship in two ways: it gives employees knowledge of the business beyond their own task, which is what allows an opportunity to be recognised at all, and the development programme itself signals that proposing change is expected rather than resented.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Intrapreneurship needs more than trained employees to appear: it needs time set aside, some budget to test an idea, a route by which a proposal reaches someone who can decide, and tolerance of proposals that fail, because a business that penalises unsuccessful ideas tends to stop receiving any.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For the business, intrapreneurship can produce a stream of improvements and new products from people who already understand its customers and its operations, at lower cost and lower risk than buying innovation from outside; against that, time spent on proposals is time not spent on current output, and most proposals do not succeed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Multi-skilling is training employees to carry out several different tasks or jobs rather than one, so that any one employee can be used in more than one part of the operation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Multi-skilling gives a business flexibility: employees can be moved to whichever part of the operation demand has risen in, absence and holidays can be covered without hiring extra staff, and a single absence is less likely to stop a process.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Multi-skilling costs more in training time and often in pay, because employees who hold several skills have more alternatives and can ask for more; it can also reduce depth, since time spent learning a second task is time not spent becoming expert at the first.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flexibility from multi-skilling is worth most where demand moves between parts of the operation or the team is small, because a small team has no spare capacity to absorb an absence; in a large operation with many employees on each task, cover already exists and the training spending buys less.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cooperation between management and the workforce means the two sides working through consultation, shared information, joint problem-solving and agreed procedures, rather than dealing with each other only when there is a dispute.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employees who have been consulted about a change are more likely to accept it, because they have heard the reason for it and have had the chance to alter how it is carried out; the change then takes effect faster and with less disruption to output than one imposed without warning.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Employees doing a job see problems that management cannot see from a distance, so a business with a working channel for raising them tends to correct faults in methods, quality and safety earlier and more cheaply than one where the first sign of a problem is a customer complaint.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For employees, cooperation gives information about the position the business is in, which lets them judge what is realistically available in a pay claim, influence over how the work is organised, and an agreed procedure that protects them against decisions taken arbitrarily.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cooperation requires both sides to give something up - management gives up some speed and some freedom of decision, employees give up some scope to resist - and where one side treats consultation as a formality with no intention of changing anything, the arrangement tends to lose the trust it depends on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A trade union is an organisation of employees formed to represent their collective interests to employers, principally over pay, hours, working conditions and job security.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Collective bargaining is negotiation between an employer and a trade union over the pay and conditions of a group of employees, in which the agreement reached applies to all the employees in that group rather than being settled person by person.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For an employer, bargaining once with a union instead of individually with hundreds of employees lowers negotiating cost and produces one settlement that fixes labour costs for an agreed period, and the union gives management a reliable channel for consulting the workforce about change.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Against that, collective strength can push pay and conditions above what individual bargaining would have produced, and the possibility of industrial action gives the workforce leverage the employer has to take into account, which can slow changes to working practices.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For employees, collective bargaining supplies negotiating power that no individual holds alone and representation when a disciplinary or redundancy decision is taken, so pay, conditions and job security tend to be better than the same employees would secure individually; membership costs a subscription, the agreement binds members who voted against it, and industrial action costs pay for as long as it lasts.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How much leverage a union has depends on how easily the employer could replace the workforce and how costly a stoppage would be: where the skills are scarce and the output cannot be produced in advance and stored, a stoppage is expensive and the union's position is stronger.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The right to form a union, to bargain collectively and to take industrial action, and the procedures that must be followed first, are set by the law of each country and differ between them, so the mechanism is what this topic requires rather than the legal position of unions in any one country.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cooperation and collective bargaining are connected: a business that consults its union between pay rounds and shares information about its position tends to reach settlements with fewer disputes, because each side has a clearer view of what the other can accept.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
